questions.q: How does the QFT's defining formula, QFT|j> = (1/sqrt(N)) * Sum over k of e^(2*pi*i*jk/N)|k>, relate to the classical DFT formula from the previous lesson?
options: It is the identical mathematical expression -- the 'quantum' part is that it acts on quantum amplitudes via a unitary circuit, not that the underlying math is different
It is a completely different formula that happens to share some notation with the DFT
It only applies when j and k are both equal to zero
It replaces the complex exponential with a real-valued cosine function
questions.explain: The QFT formula is literally the DFT matrix from Lesson 5, now applied to quantum amplitudes. The genuinely new content is building a unitary circuit that reproduces it, not new math.

questions.q: What is the exact, verified result of applying the QFT to the 2-qubit basis state |1> (N=4)?
options: 0.5|0> + 0.5i|1> - 0.5|2> - 0.5i|3>, with amplitudes cycling through the four 4th roots of unity 1, i, -1, -i
0.5|0> + 0.5|1> + 0.5|2> + 0.5|3>, the uniform superposition with no phases
1|1> and nothing else, since the QFT leaves basis state |1> unchanged
0.25|0> + 0.25|1> + 0.25|2> + 0.25|3>, with every amplitude equal to 0.25
questions.explain: QFT|1> is exactly row/column 1 of the verified 4x4 DFT matrix: amplitudes 0.5, 0.5i, -0.5, -0.5i, cycling through the 4th roots of unity e^(2*pi*i*k/4) for k=0,1,2,3.

questions.q: Why does QFT|0> come out as the perfectly uniform superposition 0.5|0> + 0.5|1> + 0.5|2> + 0.5|3>, with no phase differences at all?
options: Setting j=0 in the formula makes every exponential term e^(2*pi*i*0*k/N) equal e^0 = 1 regardless of k, so every output amplitude is weighted identically
Because |0> is defined to be immune to all quantum operations
Because the QFT circuit always initializes every qubit to |0> first, erasing any input
This result only holds by coincidence for N=4 and would differ for other values of N
questions.explain: When j=0, the exponent 2*pi*i*jk/N is 0 for every k, so every term in the sum contributes the same amplitude 1/sqrt(N) -- this holds for any N, not just N=4.

questions.q: What does rewriting j in binary fraction notation (0.j_l j_{l+1}...j_n) accomplish in the QFT derivation?
options: It allows QFT|j> to be rewritten as a tensor product of single-qubit states, each carrying one phase that depends on a suffix of j's bits -- which is exactly what makes an efficient quantum circuit possible
It converts the QFT into a purely classical algorithm with no quantum circuit needed
It eliminates the need for any complex numbers in the QFT formula
It only works for 2-qubit registers and cannot be generalized to larger n
questions.explain: The product-form derivation factors QFT|j> into a tensor product of n single-qubit states. Because the result is separable (not entangled across all qubits at once), it can be built one qubit and one controlled gate at a time -- this is the algebraic fact Lesson 7's circuit relies on.

questions.q: Why does the lesson emphasize that the QFT output 'factors' into a tensor product of single-qubit states, rather than treating this as a minor technical detail?
options: Because if the output did not factor this way, there would be no shortcut to an efficient circuit -- the fact that it factors is precisely why an O(n^2)-gate circuit construction (covered next) is possible at all
Because factoring is only relevant for error correction, not circuit construction
Because non-factored states are always faster to measure than factored ones
Because the tensor product form was historically discovered before the summation formula
questions.explain: A state that factors into single-qubit pieces can be built directly by a circuit, qubit by qubit. If the QFT output were an irreducibly entangled combination with no such factorization, there would be no efficient gate-based construction -- this is the algebraic foundation for Lesson 7.
